Based on the healthcare Q&A matches, it appears that high-dose radiotherapy may provide some benefits for palliative lung cancer patients, but the evidence is not conclusive. Some studies suggest that palliative treatment with a total dose of 25 Gy applied in 5 fractions can be sufficient to treat radiation of lung cancer, although there was no obvious survival improvement.

However, other studies indicate that external radiotherapy may be more effective than high-dose radiotherapy for palliative management of gallbladder carcinoma. Additionally, older patients with metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC) did not benefit from surgery in addition to radiotherapy regarding functional outcome, local control of MSCC, or survival.

A geriatric oncology consultation led to a modification of the cancer treatment plan in more than one third of cases. The results suggest that self-reported health-related quality of life provides independent prognostic information for survival, which supports the collection of such data in routine clinical practice.

It is essential to note that the evidence for high-dose radiotherapy as a benefit for palliative lung cancer patients is limited and inconclusive. Further studies are necessary to determine whether this treatment approach improves outcomes for these patients.

In summary, while some studies suggest benefits for palliative radiotherapy, other evidence indicates that other approaches may be more effective, and older patients with MSCC did not benefit from surgery in addition to radiotherapy. Therefore, the current evidence does not strongly support high-dose radiotherapy as a benefit for palliative lung cancer patients.
